Mitigation should proceed without asserting a root cause until the open checks are completed.

The api-gateway error rate (~8%) is lower than checkout (~21%) because api-gateway's error rate is computed over all routes, while the checkout failures affect only the checkout path; this is consistent with the checkout failures being concentrated on POST /api/v1/checkout.

Health checks for payment-service and checkout-service were healthy at 16:28Z, while payment-provider was reported degraded for elevated Charges API error rates at the same time. That makes the external provider a plausible lead, but the health checks are shallow and do not prove the cause.

Dependency edges: checkout-service calls payment-service (sync_http); payment-service calls payments-db (database) and payment-provider (external_http).

Health at 16:28Z: checkout-service healthy (HTTP /health 200); payment-service healthy (HTTP /health 200); payments-db healthy (SELECT 1 ok); payment-provider degraded, status page 'Elevated error rates on Charges API (investigating)'.

Past incident P06 (2026-06-11) had checkout 5xx errors from an expired TLS certificate on payment-service, caused by a cert-manager misconfiguration. Past incident P07 (2026-08-08) had payment timeouts from payments-db connection exhaustion.

Checkout 5xx would then propagate from payment-service. The timing has not been verified against the alert start (~16:00Z).
The v3.1.3 deploy on 2026-09-03 is a weak lead: it is about 30 hours before onset and concerns refund flow, not the authorization path. Nothing in the data links it to the egress or ingress TLS path.

An expired or unrotated certificate on the payment-service egress or ingress path remains possible, as in P06. No certificate record was found to support or rule it out, and the healthy shallow /health checks do not exercise outbound TLS, so this cannot be excluded.
The payments-db connection-exhaustion pattern from P07 does not appear in this window: payments-db reports healthy, and no payment-service config change was recorded.

findings.summary: Between 15:55 and 16:30 UTC, every payment-service WARN/ERROR line for the provider call is an HTTP 503 Service Unavailable from POST api.payprovider.example/v2/charges, all at attempt 3/3. No connection, TLS, or timeout error lines appear in the window. The logs alone do not prove whether the 503s are provider responses or locally generated, because the error text does not show the origin. Error rate and p99 latency both jumped at 16:00, and the circuit breaker opened repeatedly from 16:02 on.

observations.statement: All 35 ERROR lines in the window are 'POST https://api.payprovider.example/v2/charges failed: 503 Service Unavailable (attempt 3/3)', the first at 16:00:02Z and the last at 16:30:00Z. No other status code appears in the ERROR lines.

No connection-error, TLS-handshake-error, or timeout messages appear among the 39 WARN/ERROR lines returned for payment-service in 15:55–16:30. The WARN/ERROR set was returned in full (39 matched, 39 returned).
The circuit breaker 'payment-provider' changed CLOSED -> OPEN four times, at 16:02:04, 16:10:06, 16:17:50 and 16:25:02.
Every logged 503 reports attempt 3/3, meaning all retries were exhausted. The logs show no retry-count breakdown by outcome.
payment-service error_rate was 0.17% at 15:55 and jumped to 39.13% at 16:00, peaking at 41.94% at 16:10 and at 40.88% at 16:30.
payment-service latency_p99_ms was 464.17 ms at 15:55 and rose to 9857.35 ms at 16:00, staying near 10 s through 16:30.
payment-service cpu_pct (32–34%), memory_pct (54–57%) and request_rate (58–62 req/s) stayed flat across the window with no step change at 16:00.
The 15:55 to 16:00 interval contains no ERROR or WARN lines before 16:00:02, so the first logged failure follows the metric step by about 2 s.

interpretations.statement: The 503s most likely originate at the provider (or an intermediary in front of it) rather than inside payment-service. Evidence: the message is a standard HTTP 503 from the provider endpoint, there are no local connection, TLS or timeout errors, and the ~10 s p99 latency with 503s is consistent with a degraded upstream returning errors slowly.

Local generation by the outbound client cannot be ruled out from these logs. A client-side circuit breaker or bulkhead can produce 503-like failures, and the logs do not show the response origin, the response body, or the response headers.

The logged failure count does not match the metrics. The 35 ERROR lines are far fewer than 40% of ~60 req/s would imply (~24 failures/s), so the logs are probably sampled or aggregated. Failure counts should not be taken from these lines.

data_gaps: No outbound-client metrics were available: no per-status-code request counts, no connection-error, TLS-error or timeout counters, and no retry-attempt histogram. This query covered only payment-service's own metrics and logs, not the outbound-client breakdown the task asked for.

Log volume (35 ERROR lines) does not reconcile with the 40% error rate at ~60 req/s, so the log sample is incomplete or aggregated.
No provider-side telemetry (api.payprovider.example status or latency) was available to confirm whether the 503s are provider responses.

The api-gateway v7.4.2 TLS upgrade (C01) predates onset by six days with no trigger identified, so it is weak. Health checks at 16:28Z are shallow and do not contradict a payment-path fault. critique.summary: H-A is plausible: payment-service logs show outbound charge failures with 503 from 16:00:02Z, before the first checkout and gateway 502s, and the 502s line up with that. But the 0.60 confidence rests on the attribution of the 503s to the external provider, which no record confirms. Payment-service's own outbound client, TLS path, and payments-db (P06/P07 patterns) remain untested, and the only contradicting health check is shallow. Confidence should be lower until payment-service outbound metrics or provider-side status are obtained.

issues.detail: The analysis treats the 503s as genuine external provider responses. The ledger shows only payment-service's own ERROR lines reporting a failed outbound call; no provider-side log, status page, or payment-service outbound status breakdown was retrieved. A local outbound client, connection pool, or TLS fault in payment-service could produce the same logged failure, so the provider origin is an assumption, not an observation.

A payment-service-internal fault (outbound client, certificate, or payments-db exhaustion as in P06/P07) fits the same timeline: all failures start at 16:00 and retries are exhausted at attempt 3/3 inside payment-service. Nothing in the ledger separates a provider outage from a local cause, and the analysis lists these only as remaining gaps.

Confidence 0.60 is high given that no payment-service metrics, provider data, or payment-path health checks were obtained. The health checks cited as contradicting (H11) are shallow /health probes and carry little weight, so the contradiction is not really ignored, but the confidence should reflect the missing discriminating evidence.

The certificate hypothesis is scored low on the basis that a provider response is not genuine, which is an unverified assumption. Its support from P06 is a past incident and is not evidence that the current failure is a certificate problem. No certificate expiry record was checked.

Decisive evidence is obtainable with the available tools: payment-service outbound error and latency metrics by status code, the payments-db pool metrics, and certificate expiry records for the payment-service egress path. The analysis lists these as still needed but does not request them.

The gateway TLS upgrade is ruled out mainly by the downstream-propagation argument, which is sound, but the claim that the gateway is the least likely origin is stated more firmly than the evidence warrants since the gateway's own handshake failures were not separately measured.

issues.detail: Claim that provider degradation at 16:28Z reflects the same incident starting near 16:00Z is inferred from a single status snapshot; the provider's own incident start time was not retrieved.

A locally generated 503 (outbound client or egress TLS fault) would produce the same logged signature; no outbound per-status or TLS error metrics exist to distinguish it from a provider 503. The 'attempt 3/3' pattern is consistent with a local retry loop as well as a provider outage.
Certificate expiry and rotation checks were never returned, so the certificate hypothesis is untested rather than weakened; its 0.20 confidence rests on no data.

Flat payments-db connection counts do not exclude a payment-service-side outbound client pool, which is not visible; the analysis correctly notes this but then assigns 0.12 with contradicting evidence that only covers the DB pool.

The original analysis lists the 0.50 confidence as moderate, but the 0.80 onset inference relies on 5-minute metric resolution and log timestamps only; the causal direction (downstream origin) is stronger than the evidence shows.

analysis.response_to_critique: Missing-evidence point accepted: the outbound per-status and provider feed were not retrieved, so H-A stays at 0.50 and is explicitly assumption-dependent. The alternative-not-ruled-out point is accepted; the local-503 possibility is retained as an assumption in H-A and as H-C/H-B. The H-B certificate hypothesis is now acknowledged as untested rather than weakened, which is why its confidence rests on no data. The H-C misread point is accepted: flat DB metrics do not exclude an unseen outbound client pool. The overconfidence point is accepted: the 0.80 onset inference was lowered in reasoning to reflect 5-minute resolution and log-only timing. The provider-timing unsupported claim is accepted: the 16:28Z snapshot is treated as consistent with, not proof of, a 16:00Z incident start.

critique.summary: H-A (provider-side 503s from api.payprovider.example causing payment-service failures that propagate to checkout and gateway) is well supported by the earliest-timestamp ordering and the provider's own degraded status at 16:28Z. However, the analysis overstates confidence: the 503s are not shown to be provider responses rather than locally generated, the provider degradation is a single snapshot without a start time, and the cited contradiction H11 (healthy shallow health check) does not actually contradict H-A. Certificate and pool hypotheses remain only weakly excluded, and the 'payment-provider degraded' record was not weighed as direct support. No further investigation is possible, so the conclusion should be revised to reflect moderate confidence and explicit remaining uncertainty.

issues.detail: Confidence 0.50 is stated, but the reasoning text says 'moderate at best'. The provider status feed corroborates external degradation at 16:28Z, which supports a higher figure, yet the origin of the 503s is unverified; the calibration should be stated explicitly and consistently.

The hypothesis rests on the 503s being genuine provider responses, which is listed as an assumption. No telemetry distinguishes provider-returned 503s from locally generated ones; the only evidence is the log text, which does not show origin. The provider status page alone does not establish that these particular responses came from the provider.

The analysis lists H11 as contradicting H-A, but H11 is a shallow /health 200 check that cannot detect charge-path failures; it does not contradict the hypothesis and should not be counted against it.

Local outbound-client failure (e.g. a client-side circuit breaker or bulkhead returning 503-like errors) fits the same log signature, has the same onset, and shows the 10 s p99 with fast-fail behaviour. Without outbound-client metrics this alternative is not excluded, so H-A cannot be treated as the sole cause.

Certificate hypothesis is kept at 0.20 with P06 as the pattern, but no certificate record was retrieved and the health check is shallow; the prior incident is analogy only and should not be treated as evidence. Low confidence is appropriate, but the supporting list cites P06 as if it were evidence of current state.
Flat payments-db connection count and absent pool log lines are cited, but the pool maximum is not visible, so the contradiction is weaker than stated; confidence 0.12 is reasonable.

The api-gateway TLS library upgrade (C01, six days earlier) and the search deploy (C09) are described as weak; the search deploy is correctly deprioritised, but the gateway TLS change was not checked against the checkout path, so it remains untested rather than excluded.
